toc.title: Everyone is stuck on some level
From conscious skill to second nature
When safety has to come first

blocks.p: Is pendulation always a conscious effort, or do some people just do it naturally? And what does that mean for those who are in a stuck state?

I got a question from an [Unstucking Academy](https://www.stucknotbroken.com/checkout/co-regulator) student. She asked: does pendulation naturally occur for people who have never been stuck? And for those who are stuck, can pendulation occur naturally after learning and practicing it?
A really, really good question. Before I go into it, let's clarify what we mean by pendulation and what we mean by stuck.

Pendulation is the skill of mindfully and intentionally shifting between safety and defensive activation. On a deep, body-based level, it looks like connecting with safety activation, like a feeling of warmth in your chest from joy, and also connecting with defensive activation, like an empty void in your belly from depression.
As you permit these states and shift your focus between the two, the intensity of the depression experience softens.

Pendulation can also open the capacity, the potential, for self-regulation and for actually releasing stuck defense. Not just softening it, but maybe releasing it, or ladder climbing: [Polyvagal ladder](piece:autonomic-nervous-system) climbing.

The safety half of pendulation keeps the defensive half contained, or at a minimum. But it also helps you connect with that defense mindfully. And once you're connected with defense, as long as the safety state holds, the stuck defense can start to shift.

blocks.why: This article talks about mindfulness. This practice gives you a few minutes of it.

blocks.p: Stuck means one is chronically in defensive activation, like stuck in shutdown, which would show up as the depression emotion, like that void in the belly.

This person has less access to their safety state. Their safety state is less developed, and therefore they're not able to self-regulate. That safety state can't contain or utilize the defensive activation, so defense is too dominant. In order to self-regulate, they would need a strong enough safety state, something that's called the vagal brake in Polyvagal terminology.

So my answer to these two questions is yes. Pendulation will naturally occur for someone who's not stuck, sort of. And pendulation will naturally occur as someone gets less stuck after learning and practicing pendulation, sort of.

Let's start with an analogy that I think really helps to clarify this. You know those carnival games where you punch a bag or slam a mallet and try to get the meter to reach the top? Think of that top as the maximum capacity of your nervous system. It's the upper limit of what your system can handle before it goes into a full-blown defensive state.

People with strong enough self-regulation, those who might say they've never been stuck in the same way that a traumatized person has, have a much higher top. Their nervous system has a broader window of tolerance, a greater capacity for what it can handle. Their vagal brake, the strength of their safety state, is stronger. In large part, I would assume, that's due to good enough parenting, good enough co-regulation, and safe enough environments with safe enough others.

So when they encounter a potential trigger, which would be the punch to the bag or the mallet hitting the target, the level of dysregulation on that meter doesn't reach the highest point. It doesn't reach their top. It might go up a bit, and they would feel some discomfort, but it doesn't push them into a prolonged defensive state that they can't recover from relatively quickly.

For this person with healthy regulation, a conscious, deliberate pendulation skill isn't necessary, because their system has enough inherent capacity to process and to return to ventral vagal safety without that intentional, explicit effort. They can handle the trigger and recover from it quickly. They don't need to recall the pendulation skill and go through the steps. Their body can simply tolerate and recover from that potential trigger. For example, they'll feel activation when someone cuts them off on the road, but that's kind of the extent of it. They'll recover and move on with life.

So does natural pendulation occur for this person? Yes, it does, but it's not always the same kind of back and forth between an activated defensive state and a consciously anchored safety state that we teach when someone is stuck, like I do, or like in something like Somatic Experiencing.

Think about grieving, for example. When someone's experiencing loss and they're grieving, they will naturally enter defensive activation, various defensive states. They might cry intensely. They might feel anger or experience deep sadness. But then, without really conscious effort, they'll shift. They might remember a specific funny moment with the person they lost and spontaneously laugh, or feel a wave of warmth from a shared memory as they grieve with a family member.

Then they'll dip back into tears or anger. This crying and laughter duality, this vacillation between defense and safety, is a very natural pendulation process. The key here is that even in their grief, they have a strong enough underlying safety state, enough ventral vagal capacity, that their system can access these moments of connection and regulation even though they have a lot of pain. And so the body naturally pendulates and carries them through the grieving process.

blocks.h: Everyone is stuck on some level

blocks.p: Let's pause here and discuss stuckness again, if you don't mind the quick detour.
Everyone is stuck on some level. Literally, nobody had perfect parenting. Literally nobody had a perfectly safe environment to grow up in.

The rich, privileged stranger kid that you think had it all? Their parents didn't pay attention to them. They're filled with emptiness. They drink to feel better, and they lack real friendships. Your friend in school who seemed to have it together? They didn't. They were going through some horrible stuff in secret. How about your favorite politician that you think cares deeply about you and the community? They don't. It's all a mask they put on, focusing on fulfilling their insatiable egos so that they can ignore the pains inside.

Everyone has some level of stuckness. It's a spectrum. At one end is the perfectly regulated person who can roll with everything that fortune gives or takes away from them. This person does not exist. It's not me. It's not the spiritual guru that you're going to listen to or read next. This person does not exist.
At the other end of the spectrum is the extremely dysregulated person. This person is filled with rage, panic, fear, and is maybe even hardly functional. This person does exist.
I assume, and I hope, that most people receive good enough parenting and live in safe enough environments, but that hope is maybe, and probably, very unfounded on a global level.

I assume most people fall into the category of having some self-regulation: not in a constant state of overwhelm, but not truly thriving either. Most people are getting by, often operating on the fringes of their capacity, of what their nervous system can handle, perhaps constantly on the edge of dysregulation. They're always there, but not quite there. Many people have moments of dysregulation, like a panic attack here and there, but they can function. They have enough regulation.

But everyone has some level of stuckness, and everyone can benefit from learning new self-regulation skills, I believe. Literally everyone, even the person who wouldn't say they have trauma. I promise you, based on 17-plus years of therapy and a few years of coaching people one-on-one: even if someone doesn't have PTSD or C-PTSD, they can still benefit from the pendulation skill.

blocks.h: From conscious skill to second nature

blocks.p: I think many people have enough safety in their system to learn new self-regulation skills like pendulation. And I think they would be absolutely shocked to see how much pain, resentment, stress, hurt, and otherwise malcontent they're actually holding onto.

Maybe they don't know how to pendulate, but they can be walked through it, like during a workshop or a meditation. And through successfully pendulating, this person can increase that top on their carnival game meter.

With consistent practice, this conscious pendulation, learning the skill and implementing it as a series of steps, can eventually become subconscious. It's just like learning how to drive a car or play an instrument. Initially, it requires focus and deliberate action. It might involve remembering and following a skill sequence. When I teach pendulation, students learn the skill and then follow along with one or more of my guided meditations, but eventually I challenge them to enact the skill on their own.

By that time, it requires less conscious effort, and it could become second nature. In general, as the neural pathways strengthen and the nervous system learns this new way of being, it becomes more automatic, more integrated. Your system learns that it can move in and out of discomfort safely, and that it can return to a state of regulation.

It builds a new, higher top on that meter for its capacity, making those deep, stuck defensive states less frequent and less intense. Someone who is stuck but not traumatized, who has okay regulation, can learn pendulation and go from just getting by to genuinely expanding their nervous system's capacity for calm and confidence and connection. I think a lot of people are like that. It's about transforming that conscious effort into an embodied, automatic practice over time, much like those who've always had that strong enough baseline regulation.

blocks.h: When safety has to come first

blocks.p: For others who are more chronically dysregulated and fit the typical PTSD or C-PTSD traumatized mold, they need to establish a strong enough safety baseline.

That in and of itself may be a challenge, one with a lot of benefit, but it's a challenge. They need to get accustomed to what safety feels like, and again, that's quite a challenge for many. This person with more chronic dysregulation typically lacked effective co-regulation in childhood, and/or safe enough environments then, or even now.

So asking this person to pendulate is too big an ask. Instead, we need to focus on safety: recognizing safety, practicing how to access safety, building it, and then gently tiptoeing into defensive activation to eventually pendulate.

Can this person learn, practice, and be so successful with a skill like pendulation that it becomes second nature? Yes, I think so, generally. But it's work, and it would take a lot of patience. I think it's possible.

For those with high enough nervous system capacity, conscious pendulation as we teach it isn't always necessary, because their system manages activation differently, more effectively. Natural pendulation does occur, as in the process of grieving, where a strong safety state allows for more fluid movement between defense and safety.

For those of us who have felt stuck, or have been getting by, consciously learning and practicing pendulation is how we build that capacity, expand our window of tolerance, or raise that top on the meter, and ultimately move toward a place where pendulation can become a more subconscious, integrated part of our daily lives.
For those in a more traumatized state, with more dysregulation, yes, pendulation is a possibility, eventually, after working on safety and slowly working toward defense.
